about: Talking to a Brick Wall shows a young man in a black T-shirt standing inches from a red brick wall, hands up mid-gesture, earnestly explaining something to it. The wall, of course, gives him nothing back. The image captures the exhausting feeling of making the same point over and over to someone who will never listen: a stubborn relative, a manager, a customer service bot. Labeling the wall and the speaker turns it into a quick complaint about whoever refuses to engage, while the man's sincere body language makes his effort look both noble and pointless.
origin: The image comes from a 2010 YouTube comedy skit by Maronzio Vance in which he holds a one-sided political conversation with a brick wall to show how arguing politics can feel. The still later spread as a reaction image.
usage:
The first box sits over the wall: label the person or thing that won't listen ("management", "my grandma", "the referee"). The second box goes near the man: describe what you keep trying to explain ("me explaining why we need tests").

The more reasonable the explanation and the more immovable the wall, the better it lands. It suits workplace frustration, family tech support, group chats, sports arguments and any debate that has been had a hundred times. Keep the wall's label to a word or two so the brick texture still shows.
